June 21, 1967

speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Secretary of Stale):
subtopic: ELIGIBILITY OF NON-CANADIANS TO SEEK ELECTION
speechtext:
I am informed by the Chief Electoral Officer as follows:
Amongst other qualifications, the Canada Elections Act requires an elector to be a Canadian citizen or other British subject. In the case of a British subject other than a Canadian citizen, he must have been ordinarily resident in Canada for the 12 months immediately preceding polling day. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-MEETING BETWEEN PRESIDENT JOHNSON AND PREMIER KOSYGIN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in facing the serried ranks of the cabinet, it is difficult to know to whom the question should be placed, but I assume it should be addressed to the genial Minister of National Defence. I should like to ask him two questions, the first of which is whether the government of Canada is doing everything it can in the interests of world peace to impress upon the President of the United States the imperative need of a meeting with Premier Kosygin in New York?

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-MEETING BETWEEN PRESIDENT JOHNSON AND PREMIER KOSYGIN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in reply to this first question I can assure my right hon. friend and the house that the government of Canada is doing everything it can in the interests of world peace in attempting to bring together the four great powers to discuss the problems which are facing the world at this moment. The Prime Minister has made this position very clear and has already in private discussions with the leaders of some of our allies urged upon them the importance of the great powers getting together, preferably within the confines of the United Nations, but in any event getting together, to discuss the problems of the Middle East and how they might be reconciled.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-MEETING BETWEEN PRESIDENT JOHNSON AND PREMIER KOSYGIN
speechtext: May I repeat the first question. I did not ask anything about the Big Four meeting. I asked whether the Canadian government was impressing upon the President of the United States, Canada being one of the closest friends of the United States, the need of meeting with Premier Kosygin.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-MEETING BETWEEN PRESIDENT JOHNSON AND PREMIER KOSYGIN
speechtext: I know that the Prime Minister discussed this question with the President earlier in the context of the Big Four meeting. I cannot say specifically whether there has been conversation in the last day or two following Mr. Kosygin's statement at the United Nations; but I will be glad to refer this question to the Prime Minister and to suggest that it would be desirable to urge upon the President the desirability of a meeting if it can possibly be arranged.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-MEETING BETWEEN PRESIDENT JOHNSON AND PREMIER KOSYGIN
speechtext: Thank you.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-MEETING BETWEEN PRESIDENT JOHNSON AND PREMIER KOSYGIN
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. It is reported that the Secretary of State for External Affairs had a meeting with Premier Kosygin very recently. subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-MEETING BETWEEN PRESIDENT JOHNSON AND PREMIER KOSYGIN
speechtext: I am afraid that I have no information in this respect, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the Secretary of State is imbued with her usual geniality, may I ask her if she would indicate the arrangements which have been made for the participation of the public in the July 1 centennial celebrations on parliament hill when Her Majesty the Queen is to be present. I should be very happy to do this. Having only just received this information, I wish to say this: The information is that on the morning of July 1 there will be two

About 700,000 Canadians or 57 per cent of the 1,240,000 old age security pensioners are now receiving the guaranteed income supplement. Some 430,000 are receiving the full $30 supplement and the average for those receiving less than the maximum is approximately $18.95 per month. From this experience my department is now forecasting expenditures of $240 million in 1967-68.
The administration of this program has been handled by the staff of the old age security directorate of the department with the addition of a corps of casual employees for the initial steps of mailing, receiving and processing applications. The local offices of the Canada Pension Plan, National Revenue and the Unemployment Insurance Commission were made available to assist pensioners in making application.
The Canada Assistance Plan, enacted by parliament on July 15, 1966, to have effect from April 1, 1966, is a comprehensive measure for sharing the cost of public assistance and welfare assistance with the provinces and municipalities, with a view to encouraging the provision of adequate assistance and the improvement of services that have a preventive and rehabilitative emphasis. The act emphasizes the need for adequate assistance to be provided to persons in need and gives special emphasis to the development of welfare services which have as their object the lessening, removal or prevention of the causes and effects of poverty, child neglect, or dependence on public assistance. It thus goes beyond the concept of assistance as such and places major emphasis on the importance of prevention and rehabilitation.

Agreements were forwarded to the provinces for signature in February and to date nine provinces have entered into agreements and it is expected that the agreement with the remaining province will be concluded in the very near future.
The Canada Pension Plan began operation on January 1, 1966, when the initial contributions became payable. The first retirement pensions were paid in January of this year and, as of April 30, there were 4,449 Canadians receiving retirement pensions. It is estimated that, by the end of 1967, 18,000 Canadians will be receiving this pension and, by the end of 1968, 40,000. The organization of the Canada Pension Plan administration has progressed to the point where 37 district offices of the administration are open on a full time basis. In addition, services are provided as required in 89 local offices of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the Department of Manpower and Immigration. By combining the offices of these three agencies, we are able to provide a nationwide network of service to the public.
Work is proceeding within the Canada Pension Plan administration on survivors' benefits which are scheduled for payment for the first time in February, 1968. Current planning involves an intensive and detailed study of all provisions in the legislation relating to these benefits, drafting of regulations, the adaptation of certain procedures already developed for administration of retirement pensions, the development of procedures unique to survivors' benefits and a specialized training course for staff in the administration of this important aspect of the Canada Pension Plan. Further planning and organization in relation to the administration of disability pensions, effective in May, 1970 will proceed on schedule.

A fund of $500 million is now avail-ble for a carefully phased program extending over a 15 year period.
Preliminary programs for the development of health training facilities over the next five years have been submitted by the provinces. Supply-Health and Welfare officials have continued consultation with provincial officials and a federal-provincial conference was held several weeks ago. From all indications it would appear that the provinces are proceeding with the necessary action to complement federal legislation, thereby making possible a nation wide system of prepaid medical care.
Let me now refer to the subject of mental retardation. As one of the top ranking causes for disability among all age groups, mental retardation is regarded as a major national health, social and economic problem. It is responsible for immeasurable and prolonged frustration and loss to the retarded individual's family as well as a great loss in economic output to society.
The government has recognized that mental retardation is of national concern and warrants increased financial support for programs specifically designed to prevent and alleviate this disability.
Several avenues have been explored to date. For example, under our grants to welfare and related organizations program, the annual contribution towards the administrative and general costs of the Canadian Association for Retarded Children started at $5,000 in 1959-60 and has been increased over the last few years to $40,000. Mr. Chairman, I should like to compliment the minister for his lengthy remarks in respect of the various activities of his department and for indicating to us what has been done, what he thinks has been done and what he hopes to accomplish. There has been considerable legislation passed in respect of health and welfare in the last three years, although some of it has taken a long time to implement, such as the medicare plan. I realize there have been problems, for example the lack of funds, and this can be readily understood when one considers that we are faced with the second greatest deficit, perhaps the greatest before the year is over, in peacetime. This has been accompanied by the highest cost of living and the highest taxes in our history.
Perhaps some of these measures should have been delayed. For that reason, I should like to ask the minister to give us an indication about legislative priorities. The minister also referred to the Canada Assistance Plan and other social welfare legislation.
I do not believe there has been a yardstick devised in respect of the sharing of costs which has been acceptable both to the federal and provincial governments. Let me illustrate my point. In the province of Ontario, as well as in others, the minimal income groups are covered by medical insurance. The provincial government pays 50 per cent of the costs and we find the federal government does not enter the picture and pay the other 50 per cent. I have drawn it to the attention of this house on more than one occasion that another group of our citizens, representing about 30 per cent of our population require medical coverage that they cannot finance. Why does the government not help the provinces in this regard? If the minister is as sincere as he sounds, and as I think he is, it seems reasonable to expect the federal government would do something in this regard rather than continue this wasteful duplication through


bureaucratic practices that does not touch those marginal people when they are ill.
I should like to ask what has happened so far as the Canada Assistance Plan is concerned. We have set up boards which act as tribunals to which people can appeal if they feel they have been badly treated. I want to put on the record a case which came to my attention of a woman who had suffered severe physical and psychological trauma a few years ago. According to the manpower branch she is unemployable and certified as such. She is too old and unsuitable for retraining, yet this woman is not eligible for benefits under the Canada Assistance Plan. She has applied and has been refused. We may have the best social legislation in the world, but if it founders in a morass of bureaucracy it is not only useless, it is expensive.
Let me give another illustration of the jungle of bureaucracy in which the government finds itself. I received a report of a man who is 64 years of age and who served in two world wars. He did not get out of Canada during the last one but he was with the Queen's Own Rifles in Newfoundland training troops there for overseas duty. This man became paralysed after a stroke. He could not talk or get out of bed. His Ontario hospital insurance ran out and he was told he would have to get out of the hospital. At that time the case was drawn to my attention and I referred it to the Ontario Hospital Commission. They felt that something could surely be done.

But all that was done was to tell this man to go home, where his wife was ill and waiting for a bed in hospital. This is an example of how well some of the programs have worked. The Ontario Hospital Commission said this man was a veteran and came under the Department of Veterans Affairs at Ottawa. They said the department should look after him since he was in the first world war. This fellow could not speak. He had lost his papers and number. Remember he was also in the second world war. When this matter was taken up with the authorities they said he had never been out of Canada. He was in Newfoundland, Mr. Chairman, and Newfoundland was not part of Canada in 1942, 1943, 1944 and 1945.
I bring this case to the attention of the minister to point out the loopholes in the hodge-podge welfare legislation that has been brought before this house and passed. I do not
June 21, 1967

wonder that the minister wants to have a guaranteed income established because that will be the only way out of this jungle in which he finds himself. What happened to this man? They refused to treat him as a veteran. They said he did not qualify to enter Sunnybrook because he had not been out of Canada.
Then I called the local welfare department which finally took over the case and this man is today under custodial care. I bring this case to the attention of the minister to point out that there was a failure, not only at the provincial level but at the federal level as well. There was also a failure at the local level of communication. We have not much to boast about when a man who is defenceless, cannot get out of bed and cannot even talk, is treated in this way. I would point out that this man enlisted in the first world war when he was in his teens.
1 could tell the minister about dozens of other cases where the same problem has arisen. It is because of these problems that the other day the minister of welfare said we will have to set up a system or committee whereby these people can be interviewed and assisted when refused help. What is wrong with the local authorities, the provincial governments and the federal government? Is there no co-operation or co-ordination so that a man will have his case fairly appraised? This type of wasteful bureaucracy must not be permitted. We in this country may be well off, but we are not that well off. We cannot afford all this duplication and waste, and at the same time pay the high costs of administration. I have referred specifically to this government but I suppose all governments are doing the same thing in a smaller way. We added 12,000 civil servants to the bureaucracy last year. There comes a time when bureaucracy should no longer be enlarged. Very soon we will have more chiefs than Indians, more civil servants than taxpayers.
I wish to spend a few minutes dealing with the problem of mental and tuberculosis hospitals. I ask the federal government why they categorize a man as a second class citizen because he is a mental patient. Is it not about time that in this Canada of ours we regarded a mentally ill person as being in the same category as a person who is physically ill? Just as many beds are occupied in this country today by the mentally ill as the physically ill. The federal government, despite all its magnanimity and its great welfare programs, will not provide assistance for the care of the mentally ill.
Supply-Health and Welfare
There are many blind areas in our welfare programs. The attitude toward the mentally sick is one of them. Why is the stigma of a second class citizen attached to a person who unfortunately becomes mentally ill? A mentally ill person is just the same as any other ill person. The only difference is that he becomes nervous and emotionally upset, instead of requiring his appendix to be taken out or having some other medical problem. The same thing applies to our tubercular patients, who fortunately are becoming less in number. It would not cost a great deal of money to include the cost of care of the mentally sick and our tubercular patients. The cost of a bed in a mental hospital is approximately one third of the cost of a bed for the medically ill or the person requiring surgery.
In this connection, I make a plea on behalf of the provinces. In the province of Ontario expenses rose 25 per cent last year. The federal government, with all the taxing powers it has, last year had an increase in expenses of only 14 per cent. I have a great deal of sympathy with the provinces. It is sometimes said the provinces are creating problems by saying they are not being fairly treated. This is a very good illustration of the fact that they are not being fairly treated. At the provincial level, expenditures are increasing much faster than they are at the federal level.
We must also remember that administrative costs fall entirely upon the province that administers the program. The federal government says it shares these costs of welfare 5050. This is not so, because administration is entirely an expense of the province. The federal government will not even be sharing medicare costs 50-50 with the province of Ontario. It will be contributing much less than 50 per cent.
On the subject of psychiatric care in Canada, Dr. Alex Richmond said there was the greatest need to see that these people get adequate care, not only from the standpoint of the federal government accepting its share but in helping to get these people rehabilitated as quickly as possible. The longer a person stays in a mental hospital, the less his chance of complete recovery.
Then, there is the problem of alcoholism. About 2 per cent of the population today suffer from alcoholism; the number is around 400,000. Should not the costs incurred in treating these unfortunate people be shared equally by the federal government, which obtains very large sums of money in the way of
June 21, 1987

Supply-Health and Welfard taxes from the sale of alcohol? Last year more alcohol was sold in this country than ever before. I ask, should the federal government not also assist people suffering from other forms of addiction?
I ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare why he does not go a little further than his predecessors and accept some responsibility in these fields. The treatment of these people should be accepted as a federal responsibility under a shared program. These people are Canadians; they are sick, and need treatment. With regard to shared programs, those provinces which have not the necessary funds with which to match the contribution of the federal government should be helped.
Then there is the crisis in the shortage of doctors. Not one medical university this year is providing a summer course. We will admit about 1,000 medical students to university this fall. The other day at Atlantic City the American Medical Association went on record as saying that the doctor shortage in the United States is very critical. They called for more schools. They accepted over 20,000 applications in this respect. You do not need to be a mathematician, Mr. Chairman, to figure out that this is 20 times the number we are accepting. You do not need to be a mathematician to know that the population of the United States is 10 times greater than that of Canada. On the same basis we should be accepting just double what we are, namely, 2,000.
What is being done to solve these problems? The lack of action on the part of the government is what alarms me. Has the minister taken cognizance of these problems, or does he stand back like Ferdinand brushing the flies off his back.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
When the minister brought in the medicare legislation it was his responsibility to bring in measures to aid the provinces in producing doctors because the provinces by themselves do not have the resources to do it.
Dr. Jones stated the following in speaking about the health resources fund:
Honesty compels me however to agree with the dean of every Canadian medical school and with practically every minister of health in this country, that the amount is grossly inadequate, and the fact that after two years only the very initial expenditures have been made gives point to my comments about difficult administration.
We hear nothing about the personnel to operate the hospitals. Are we to have a group of empty buildings with nobody in them? What is the use of putting up buildings if we
[Mr. Rynard.i
do not fill them with personnel and equipment? I say to the minister that it is too bad that nothing was done to ensure that our Canadian medical schools would operate this summer. I disagree entirely with the minister's opinion that we will have a sufficient number of doctors, and I challenge his statement.
Dr. Dawson stated, after a good deal of exploration across this country and after having interviewed many medical schools, that it would be necessary to bring into this country 500 doctors per year. The Hall commission report is now some years old but its recommendations have not been carried out. I want to point out to the minister that a great responsibility lies on his shoulders because he himself admitted that the implementation of medicare will increase the workload of the doctors. I agree with him.
I should like to deal now with the question of priorities in medical care, and I thank the minister for being good enough to send me his speech in which he mentioned this subject. I want to ask him, who will allocate the priorities? Who will say in what category one is to be placed so far as medical care is concerned? Is some receptionist going to decide whether or not one's appendix is to be taken out or whether one can afford to wait, two, three or four months for a doctor's care? If the minister will suggest that the emergency departments of hospitals will do it, let me tell him that they are now overloaded and overworked. There are fewer interns in the hospitals across Canada than there have been for years.
I was very interested in another point which the minister mentioned. He said that general practitioners practising in rural areas will be quite satisfied with their lot. They will be paid for the work they do and they will like living out in the country. I will tell the minister that I have had the occasion to speak to some of these doctors who told me they were having some problems. The nearest hospital is often 20 miles away and they average three or four cases in hospital because the doctors in the town are too busy. There is an insufficient number of interns in the hospitals, and yet when these doctors put in claims for mileage on their income tax forms the Department of National Revenue refuses to acknowledge them. Is one hand working with or against the other. What is the minister doing about this situation? I agree with him that we need more doctors in rural areas.
June 21, 1967

There is another point which I should like to reiterate, that is the acute shortage of doctors in this country. In the United States there are just under 300,000 doctors practising. In Canada we have just under 20,000 practising doctors.
It was pointed out at a meeting in Atlantic City the other day that an acute shortage of doctors existed in the United States. Here we are letting things ride because if we wanted it badly enough, our medical schools could have been operating this summer. Somehow or other the minister could have used his powers of persuasion, and I do not think it would have taken much persuasion, to convince the doctors of the necessity of operating the schools this summer. They could operate at increased pace, using buildings that would be empty, and instead of graduating doctors after six years they would do so after four. Dr. Evans, the head of the medical school at McMaster University, even said they could graduate a doctor in three years. He said this was a necessity, but even at that he stated we will not be able to fill the gap. I note that the minister is quoted as saying that everything will be fine here and we will have all the doctors we need in 1971 or 1972. I wonder who is right because the United States has a dire shortage of doctors and yet they have one doctor for every 750 people while we have a doctor for roughly every 1,000 people. In view of the fact that 50 per cent of our doctors are specialists we must assume there is a doctor for every 2,000 people in Canada.
I believe that things must be made a little more attractive for the general practitioners here, and the government should work in conjunction with the provincial governments and with the universities to ensure that Canadians receive the medical care which is required. I tell the minister in all frankness that 85 per cent of all illnesses can be looked after by a general practitioner, but today 50 per cent of our doctors are specialists and 50 per cent are general practitioners. The minister should consult the provinces and the universities on these very points which are so vital to Canadians so that they can obtain the best use of medical man power.
I do not believe it is right to give the people medicare and to assure them they will get all the medical care they will require when and how they like it. This would be gross misrepresentation on the part of the minister because he himself admitted it may be necessary to establish priorities in medical care. All this is very puzzling to me because I know how long some people have to wait
Supply-Health and Welfare before they can see a doctor, and yet the minister will increase the workload of the doctors without ensuring that more of them will be available.
I hope the minister and the government will face this situation squarely because it is my guess that the flow of immigration will be reduced substantially. I do not think that the European countries will continue to graduate doctors for the purpose of sending them here. Here in Canada it costs approximately $50,000 to graduate a doctor. If Great Britain and the other European countries continue to send their doctors over here, they will be giving us a real asset. I hope they do, but I doubt it.
There is another interesting point which I would like to make. What does one do if one wants to bring a doctor from Great Britain or another European country? I put this question to a government official the other day and I was told I could go to a local immigration office and ask them about it. This is the biggest farce I ever saw. One has to go to an immigration office to get a doctor to practise in a given area or to help out in a clinic. Surely, the problem of the shortage of doctors is important enough to warrant the establishment of a liaison between the Departments of National Health and Welfare and Immigration so that it would be sufficient to deal with only one department and one would not have to wander around in a maze of bureaucracy trying to get a doctor to come over to Canada.
I believe there was much sense in what the attorney general of the province of Ontario had to say. I know he was criticized and I do not agree with all he said.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
However, there was quite a lot of common sense in what he said. He noted that the provinces got together in confederation and that the federal government was the central power. But why would not the idea of bringing together the provincial ministers of health to discuss their needs, their plans and the great shortage of doctors today be appealing? Would not this advice be worth while.
I mentioned research and the necessity for more research. Dr. Thomson, who was president of the Canadian Medical Association, stated that the health resources fund provided a pittance compared with what we really need. The matter which concerned him most of all, Mr. Chairman, was how to staff the structures that the fund, spread over 15 years, builds, after it has been equalled dollar for dollar from provincial funds-that is, if the provinces can find the funds. The minister
June 21, 1967

Supply-Health and Welfare will recall that the Hall report called for a drastic increase in the supply of doctors, nurses, technicians and paramedical personnel who are required to provide adequate medical care, and this before medicare is instituted. Yet the government does nothing to bring this about. The scheme has now been put into operation and as Dr. Thomson said, the fund has provided a mere pittance.
Another aspect of the research problem is this. In order to have good teachers in the field of research you must have research-minded doctors. The medical research council is receiving just about half the amount recommended in the Gundy report. There is talk about reversing the brain drain, but I should like to see the statistics in this regard because I do not think that the drain is all that heavy. I have seen very little evidence of it. But how can we possibly bring our doctors back when we are spending a mere pittance on research.
I would call to the minister's attention that the Minister of Industry, speaking in Paris, said that 2 per cent of the gross national product should be put into research. But what do we find, Mr. Chairman? Two per cent would provide an amount of $1,200 million for research, whereas today we are spending, as the minister knows better than I, less than $26 million-about $25,800,000. As I say, this is less than half the amount that the Gundy report stated we must spend if we are to provide the doctors, personnel and trained medical students we require. This is rather pitiful in view of the situation in which we are.
Many towns across Canada have no resident doctor. As we sit here in this house more and more towns are being deserted. In the long run this is going to prove expensive because we are increasing the load on our paramedical services, ambulances and so on, who have to take care of people without their own doctor. When the doctor lives nearby most of this cost is offset. Not only that, when an ambulance is called the patient is sure to be taken to hospital which taxes the emergency department.

I appreciate the courtesy of hon. members in allowing me to go on, and I will speak for only a few minutes. I am interested in this question. I know the minister personally, and although he is a very fine fellow I am wondering whether he does have all the information that he should have. He must have been talking to a different group of fellows from those I talk to because most of the people I speak to refer to the dire shortage of medical personnel. Just the other day I heard of one man who died, I am sure, because he did not receive prompt care. There was no one available to care for him.
Another big problem in our hospitals today is this. Some people have to go to the emergency department of a hospital because they are unable to obtain the services of a doctor. People arrive in a new city and are unable to find a doctor to treat them because the doctors themselves are overworked. Therefore if they get sick they go to the emergency department of a hospital. The emergency departments of all hospitals across Canada, of which I am aware, are overloaded; the staffs are overworked and inadequate in number to do things they are supposed to do.
We can slough this off and say that the situation will correct itself and that things will be all right in a few years. But in passing through this house a medicare bill, it is not only the right of the minister but his solemn obligation to see that the people of Canada get the best medical service possible. In this vein I close. The situation is a very serious one, and I am reminded of Nero sitting fiddling while Rome burned.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is always a privilege to take part in the discussion of the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare. As usual, I have one or two complimentary remarks to make; however the minister will not be surprised if I say them quickly and get on with the meat of what I should like to say on this occasion.
I agree with the minister when he speaks of the tremendous importance of the Department of National Health and Welfare. I share his pleasure in noting that its progress, its growth and its development can be measured by the fact that its budgetary requirements have increased tenfold in the last two decades. This, I suggest, is not just an example of bureaucracy, of government spending gone wild; rather it is an indication of the demands that parliament, in the name of the people of Canada, has made for improvements in our social security program in this
June 21. 1S67

Supply-Health and Welfare stand in the way of people in the provinces getting this extra $30 under the guaranteed income supplement and continuing to get whatever the provinces want to pay to them by way of provincial supplementary allowance." That is what the minister said.
We have had many experiences in this area and I shall base what I want to say in this connection on an experience that my leader, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, had with one of his constituents. I bring this matter up because the correspondence between the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and the minister of social welfare for the province of British Columbia makes the point very clear. This was a case where a person in British Columbia was drawing $75 a month old age security and $30 a month as an extra social allowance which was paid by the province of British Columbia. She applied for the guaranteed income supplement of $30. The minister told her, the application form told her, the instruction book told her, and the act told her that she could apply for the guaranteed income supplement although she was getting the $30 a month supplement from the province of British Columbia. But what happened?
Her case was assessed by officials in British Columbia, and in the end they cut her provincial allowance down to $1.65. As the result of this great, new piece of legislation this woman who had been getting $105 a month now gets $106.65 a month.
My leader, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, did what all of us have done in our own cases. He wrote to the minister of social welfare of British Columbia, hon. Mr. Campbell, suggesting that it was improper for British Columbia to take this attitude; that, after all, the Minister of National Health and Welfare had made it clear that they were under no obligation to cut down on the provincial allowance because of what was provided in the federal legislation. The minister of social welfare for British Columbia wrote back to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam on May 19, 1967, and said this:
The quotation in your letter from my department's notice dated February 20th, 1967, is exactly as quoted. The province of British Columbia has on a number of occasions made representation to the federal government to ignore the guaranteed income supplement as income when determining entitlement to the provincial government supplementary social allowance. The result of this would have been that every recipient would have continued to receive the same amount of supplementary social allowance as he did prior to receiving the guaranteed income supplement.


It was the desire of British Columbia to continue the full amount of the supplementary social allowance paid to individuals prior to their receiving the guaranteed income supplement but the federal government refused to accept this request and stated that if the government of British Columbia ignored the guaranteed income supplement as income in determining eligibility for the provincial government supplementary social allowance that it would not share in this supplementary social allowance.
Does the minister see what he has done?

speechtext: Perfectly.

speechtext:
He has said that supplementary social allowances, as received in the provinces, do not count against the income test with respect to the guaranteed income supplement. In effect, the minister said that people could get both.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
He says it is up to the provinces whether or not they continue, but then when a province like British Columbia says it wants to continue, but in the meantime has come under the Canada Assistance Plan, this minister says, "If you are going to expect us to share in this program under the Canada Assistance Plan we will not do it unless you include the guaranteed income supplement as income for the purposes of the Canada Assistance Plan."
I take the minister back to the debate on the Canada Assistance Plan. He told us time and time again that all that mattered was that people take a needs test, and the government was prepared to leave the decision on what the level would be to provincial governments. Yet here is a case where a provincial government says it wants to pay a higher amount but the minister, through his officials, says this cannot be done because of the terms of the Canada Assistance Plan.
The minister has been reasserting this principle in recent times. He made one of his many speeches recently in Winnipeg, on June 13, and when speaking about the Canada Assistance Plan and its needs test, which he claims is so much better than a means test, he said this:
The provinces may, of course, in their discretion, impose limits on the amounts to be paid to individuals or families or for specific needs. But I emphasize again, the federal legislation leaves it to the judgment and discretion of the provinces to determine what limits, if any, should apply.
This has got to be sorted out. The minister is still saying ex post facto that the federal government imposes no limit on the amounts that may be paid under the Canada Assistance Plan. Provided people take a needs test,
June 21. 1967	COMMONS
then the federal government will pay 50 per cent. But British Columbia comes back and says, "We were denied the right to pay these social allowances unless we included as income what is being paid under the guaranteed income supplementation program."
I suggest there are two things to note here. One is the inconsistency of the position taken by the minister, and the other is that we have here another example of the fact that this idea of imposing a means test or needs test on our old people just does not fit with the thinking of today, just does not fit with the affluence we are talking about, just does not fit with the so-called just or great society.
I call upon the minister to reconsider his whole position. I suggest that if we must maintain this needs test program on old age security supplementation for a while, then things such as those to which I have just referred should be improved. But I go further than that and say that what is necessary is to change the whole basis of this supplement and put it where we tried to get it last year, on a basis as of right, whereby the full $105 per month will be paid to all who are of pensionable age and over.
There are scores of examples like this. The minister boasts about the number of people who are getting guaranteed income supplementation. But my mail, and I am sure that of many other hon. members, is just full of letters from people who are humiliated by the tests they have to go through, who are disturbed and unhappy over the reductions that take place, and who are disturbed because they do not get any supplement at all. Then, when we get a case like this where a woman gets an increase of only $1.65 per month as a result of the $30 change, and finds she is caught in this straight contradiction between the minister of Social Welfare in British Columbia and the Minister of National Health and Welfare, then I say something ought to be done about it.
I have read hon. Mr. Campbell's letter in which he says it was Ottawa that said no, that they could not do it. That was dated May 19, 1967. Yet as recently as June 13, 1967, the minister was still saying in a public address that the federal legislation leaves it to the judgment and discretion of the provinces to determine what limit if any should apply. We will come back to this later during discussion of these estimates.
I would point out that on the order paper I have a private members' notice of motion dealing with the question of removing the 27053-114

Supply-Health and Welfare means test from the $30 supplement, and I suggest to the minister that this is a piece of unfinished business with which he should be dealing without delay.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few words about medicare, to which the minister and the hon. member for Simcoe East referred. I noted that the minister today said without any embellishment at all that medicare is to come into effect on July 1, 1968. Has he forgotten that tremendous victory he secured at the meeting of the Liberals at the Chateau Laurier some time ago, when he persuaded them that he would get something better than the Minister of Finance had proposed, that he would get written into the act a provision that medicare could come into effect on July 1, 1968, or earlier? He did not mention that today. He just knows that it is not coming into effect a day earlier than July 1, 1968.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that that particular amendment which the minister put into the act just was not worth the time it took to write it out. It had no meaning, no value at all. As a matter of fact, it is like another amendment he accepted. After much pressure from all the opposition parties in the house he accepted an amendment regarding paramedical services to make it possible for the government to agree with any one province, if a province so wished, to include other than medical services under the coverage of the medicare act.
There was no question about what that amendment meant, namely, that it could be done if only one province wanted to make the agreement. When this was discussed on a late show a few weeks ago the minister freely admitted that that is the wording of the law. However, in his answer to the question on the late show he said that the law says one thing but the policy of the government is another.
The law says it can be done if even only one province wants to make such an agreement, but the minister says the policy of the government is that it is not to be done until there is a consensus. The consensus has not been defined as to whether it means two provinces, five or six, or nine or ten. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this is not the way for this minister, or any other minister on that side of the chamber, to treat this parliament. We took him seriously in the debate on the medicare bill when these two amendments were put through. One was his own, his own idea, and the other he accepted from this side of the chamber. One was that medicare might come into effect earlier than July
June 21, 1967

Supply-Health and Welfare 1, 1968, and the other was that paramedical services, such as optometry and chiropractic services, and the rest, could be included on the basis of an agreement between a province and the federal government. It now turns out that this was just so much window dressing, just a case of being agreeable to get the bill passed.

speechtext:
It is quite clear that the only service the minister had in mind at that moment was dental surgery, but it was also made very clear that the amendment as worded and put into the act did not require a consensus among the provinces for its terms to be carried out. It is this about which I am complaining, that the minister sells parliament a bill of goods by writing something into law and then says later, "That is the law. That is what can be done, but the policy of the government is something else. The policy of the government is not to act in this field unless we have a consensus." Mr. Chairman, we contend that this simply is not good enough. This is no way to treat parliament.
The minister has to give a lot more attention to this whole medicare proposition. I am sure he not only recalls his experiences in meetings recently with the Canadian Medical Association but he must also be reading the papers these days, and it must be pretty clear to him that the Canadian Medical Association is not exactly on the bandwagon in favour of medicare. The statements which are being made by the doctors about medicare do not auger well for the inauguration of this program. When one realizes the influence the medical people have at the local level and in the provinces, and when one realizes the efforts they are making, the minister may find that the program will not get off the ground as even he hopes it will. I think part of the reason for this is the delay which has taken place across the years. I believe part of it is because the minister is not as wholehearted in his determination about medicare as he ought to be. I believe right now he should be giving the fullest concentration he can to negotiations with the provinces and with the doctors in order to make sure that medicare will get off the ground certainly not later than July 1, 1968.

[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, all of us in this chamber have reason to be grateful to the medical profession. All of us have reason to be grateful to individual members of the medical profession. It seems to me, however, that they should realize that the parliament of Canada, representing the people of Canada, has spoken on this issue. The parliament of Canada has said that medical care is something which should be available to all the people of this country and that it should be paid for as provided in the act. This is no time for one group to try to sabotage this very important program.
I urge the Minister of National Health and Welfare to spend a little less time running around the country telling us how wonderful some of these programs are, for they are not as wonderful as he says. He should spend a little more time trying to make sure that the medicare program really gets going and really is the success we believe it ought to be. This should be his main preoccupation right now.
There are one or two individual matters which I should like to mention before my time runs out. These are things on which I hope we will have action at this session. I mention these because they come under the aegis of the Department of National Health and Welfare. I refer to the question of legislation on birth control and with respect to abortion. I realize the Prime Minister has made statements about these matters at political meetings outside the house. I realize also that he has included them in speeches he has made in the house. But still it seems so difficult to get from the government assurance that anything will be done.
The other night my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare for a very simple statement. In fact, she simply asked whether he could tell us if this would be done at this session. The minister could not seem to find it in his heart or in his vocabulary to say yes. Instead, he used words which may or may not have meant something. This is a social problem which we ought not to play around with any longer. There is legislation in the Criminal Code which causes a good many people such as priests, ministers, doctors and social workers, to do criminal acts because of the way the legislation now stands. There is a similar situation with respect to abortion.
These are subjects which a few years ago could not be talked about in the House of
June 21, 1967	COMMONS
Commons. Surely, however, when one thinks of the danger which exists in so many cases to the health of expectant mothers we should be prepared to deal with this question. One of the points the government has made is that in this centennial session, in the fall at any rate, we will deal with some of these social problems. Another one is in the news now. There is a scoop, I suppose you would call it, about what the committee on divorce will recommend. I do not bring this within the ambit of the Department of National Health and Welfare, but I do urge the minister in his capacity as the minister of a department concerned with the physical and mental health of our people to put the prestige and pressure he has behind the demand for action in these fields.
I shall not take the time to repeat the speech I have had to make so often about the 30, 40 or 50 years it takes the Liberal party to get anywhere. I do hope that this will not be the story in respect of these social issues which the Liberals trot out at their conventions, at election time and in the speech from the throne. Let us have action on them at this session of parliament.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I believe I can refer to just one other subject and stay within the 30 minutes allotted to me at this time. I have been quite interested in the many references the Minister of National Health and Welfare has made, when he has delivered speeches around the country, to the broad question of a guaranteed annual income. I was looking forward to hearing about this in his remarks today, but I did not hear any reference to this matter. Certainly, however, this is a favourite of his in the speeches he makes when he is receiving honorary degrees and when he is speaking to various organizations and conferences outside the house.

Supply-Health and Welfare
I suppose that "few" will always include those of us in parliament. Then the speech continues:
In simple, dramatic terms, the traditional, centuries-old link between work and income is being questioned. At the root of it all is the basic problem of how to make our nineteenth century distribution system cope with the productive machinery of the late twentieth century.
Then, after a couple of paragraphs in which he has a Munchausian reference he says:
These developments, these prospects and questions are the basis of a rising interest in the guaranteed minimum income as a radical-and realistic-solution to the problem of income distribution in the cybernetic age.
Despite the flowery nature of all that, I must say I agree that this problem of finding a basis for the right to live other than an association with work is one which will be upon us before we realize it. I agree that a guaranteed annual income is something to which we will have to come.
I should like to say first, let it not be the type of guaranteed annual income he tried to sell us in respect of the old age pensioners. First of all, the levels he had in mind did not represent a guaranteed annual income at all. Second, it is not a guaranteed annual income when it is paid to people only after they pass a needs or income test. A guaranteed annual income, if it is to be worth that name, should be a generous allowance which is sufficient for people to live on and, if it is too much, let some of it be taken back afterwards in the form of income tax.
The minister must recast his whole thinking on this issue. subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am glad to have the opportunity to say a few words about the Department of National Health and Welfare.
There are great needs in the field of social welfare, because the Canadian people are not treated as they should be, in accordance with our production. As a matter of fact, our production is high in Canada, but consumption is inadequate, because we do not consume our production. If we want to consume our production, we must at all costs balance our economy, and I do not see any other means to do so than by giving the people, the consumers themselves, in short, the families, the required purchasing power to become the great consumers of our abundant production.
Mr. Chairman, 1 do not intend to mortify the government, or the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) or the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen), but I cannot let this opportunity go by without pointing out once again, to the house, the urgent necessity of ensuring national economic balance between the individuals, the families and the institutions which compose Canada.
When I say "between the individuals, the families and the institutions", I want to point out that families and institutions are merely groups of individuals, and that human beings only are gifted with life, have material, intellectual and spiritual needs. Indeed, families and institutions are merely instruments to produce and manage in the service of human beings.
Families and institutions as such do not exist, do not have a real life; our intelligence has created them to designate groups of human beings who live together as families, or work together as institutions.
As you can see, Mr. Chairman, only human beings have life and make up a nation, are divided into families and private and public institutions, for their needs of production or administration.
Therefore, when shall we finally understand that the human being is the fundamental unit of the nation, that it represents the basic unit of any economic administration of the nation of Canada, of the country, which we have the official mandate to administer appropriately, we the 265 members of parliament with the 102 senators of Canada?

When, some day, we have recognized in our mind and by our actions that we are responsible for the good administration of the welfare of all the human beings who make up Canada, the 20,400,000 Canadians who constitute the Canadian people, then, and only then, we will have achieved the purpose for which we have been elected, for which our electors have sent us to parliament, namely to prepare legislation for all human beings, with no exception.
If it is up to the Minister of Finance to supply the necessary funds to the Department of National Health and Welfare, it is also up to the Minister of National Health and Welfare to produce his accounts which means all the accounts necessary to the economic balance of Canadian men and women, in short the 20,400,000 Canadian citizens living on Canadian soil, saluting our Canadian flag, singing our Canadian hymn and who are proud to say they are Canadian citizens.
Mr. Chairman, if, once again, there are
20,400,000	Canadian citizens who make up Canada, who have the right to live decently in Canada in 1967, it must be admitted that there are only 7,400,000 who have an income from their labour or their capital. There are 13 million other Canadian citizens who have neither capital nor paid employment, who have no personal income and who consequently are dependants.
These 13 million Canadian citizens are all entitled to live in 1967 according to our Canadian standard of living. If these 7,400,000 adult citizens are strictly entitled to a vital minimum, this vital minimum is the responsibility of the Ottawa government and must be valued in dollars and cents, according to appropriate amounts and not in a ridiculous fashion or with an eye-dropper.
This vital personal right is the right of the human beings in society and must be paid or guaranteed by the state, by the national government, by the central government, in short by the government with the financial means whether money, credit or capital, whatever their definite or indefinite forms, known or unknown, visible and invisible.
The right to live thus implies a certain amount of money daily, monthly or yearly for each Canadian citizen who has no income from his labour or his capital.
This, Mr. Chairman, is a natural human right for those who believe in God. It is a right already recognized in our Canadian legislation under chapter 44 of the Statutes of Canada 1960, the Canadian Bill of Rights.
June 21. 1967

To be practical and logical, this individual right to live must be evaluated and appraised in dollars and cents as any other contract. The salary of labour is evaluated in a definite amount, not in vague terms. Interest on capital is also evaluated in exact terms clearly determined in a contract.
In the same manner, the right to live of citizens without personal income must be spelled out by the contracting parties, in the circumstances the federal government and the dependent citizens, represented by their 265 members in the parliament at Ottawa.
Such is our responsibility as members in this House of Commons, as representatives of the people, as representatives of every Canadian citizen, as representatives above all of the weakest citizens of the country, of those who do not have the ability to defend their own cause by personal means, of the unemployed, of those who have no personal capital.
It is not a matter of knowing whether the government has the means to pay or to guarantee this right to live to the 13 million dependent Canadian citizens, it is a matter of recognizing that the government has the strict obligation to do it immediately within the present context of the Canadian monetary, economic and political machinery on the basis of the present production capacity and the standard of living of Canadians in 1967.
It is as simple as that, as complete as that. And it will be the end of the war on poverty, misery, indigence, insecurity; the end of poverty. The lack of wealth will remain, but it will be more human, more decent, more social, more natural and more proper.
As soon as we have admitted our duty to pay or to guarantee that right to a personal life to those 13 million dependent children, students or adults throughout Canada, at a set rate per month according to the cost of living index, I am ready to wager with those hardest to please that it will seem easy to them and even pleasant to proclaim the law of the right to live for all the citizens of Canada who have no personal income through their capital or their work.
The return on capital, Mr. Chairman, remains; the salary remains for all of the 7,-
400,000	persons involved in the national production. But, there is simply added the right to life for every dependent citizen as a minimum and guaranteed purchasing power, for all persons who are unemployed or who have no capital. It is as simple as that.
Supply-Health and Welfare
Everybody admits that production is for the use of the population as a whole. Everybody admits that every living individual in Canada has a right to life. Now, in 1967, we have a population of 20,400,000, and the production of the 7,400,000 producing citizens totals more than $62 billion. So we get the following averages: $62 billion; an average of 3,000 per person. Population in 1967: 20,400,000 persons; an average of $15,000 per family of five.
This is our production, the total and effective production of Canada, Mr. Chairman. And when we are told that there is not enough money to help families or to pay adequate family allowances for Canadian children, well, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that we are not equal to the task, that we are in a situation entirely different from that which exists when we say that.
It is therefore obvious that the Canadian production in 1967 can provide all dependents with a vital guaranteed minimum, in accordance with the cost of living index, as well as all families, all heads of family and all students. We could even pay a reasonable allowance to the mothers who are unemployed but who also work for the community and are not rewarded for their work.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I do not wish to complicate the present discussion, but in my opinion the 13 million citizens in Canada in 1967, whether dependents, children, students or adults, should receive a stipulated monthly payment, and I think that in order to give our society and all Canadian families their due in a country where there is an abundance of wealth, we could use $8 billion out of a national product of $62 billion, which would leave a total of $54 billion for salaries and return on capital to be paid to the 7,400,000 Canadians who contribute to the national production.
I have all sorts of tables I could quote, but that would take too long. I do not want to take up all the time of the house. I would like to give the ministers and hon. members time to think about the social welfare we could provide for Canadian families trapped in an unjust system.
It is wrong for us to tolerate such a system and to allow families to live in destitution, poverty and insecurity, as we do now while spending millions and billions of dollars for all sorts of other things. The family is the basis of the whole structure of society and of public institutions. If there were no children, no families, there would be no society, no Parliament, and we would not have to pay family allowances.
June 21, 1967

Supply-Health and Welfare
If we do not believe in the family, Mr. Chairman, the birth rate will decline. Moreover, everybody agrees that the birth rate is declining in Canada. Why? Because these families have not the security they need, because they lack the means of obtaining suitable housing, enough room, for their children.
Nobody wants to rent houses to large families; they are unable to find housing.
So, we have much to do in that area, and I say once more that we must provide families with capital and the buying power needed to purchase the production of our economy, through science, through progress, through technology. Then, Mr. Chairman, we would be doing a great service to society and also to production, because to increase production we must also increase consumption.
And statistics prove that production in Canada is plentiful since, once again, we have a production of $62 billion and a consumption of $44 billion.
Large companies in Canada have also realized profits, they have capitalized $18 billion out of $62 billion of production. We have $18 billion of capitalization; $15 billion have been capitalized by large businesses and only $3 billion by the little people.
Mr. Chairman, there might be some exaggeration in our capitalization. It is not up to me to see to it but up to the Minister of Finance and Receiver General (Mr. Sharp). And the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) should submit his bills to the Minister of Finance, so that the family may live reasonably well and properly in a country which is bursting with wealth.
If the 1967 production, in the amount of $62 billion, for a population of 20,400,000, guarantees, on the average, $3,000 per person, $250 a month, that is an average of $15,000 for a family of five (father, mother and three children) or $1,250 per month, and if such wonderful averages leave so many people in misery, in poverty, in insecurity, we must find the causes for such a poor distribution of such a large affluence.
When we see that, in 1966, out of a national production of $56 billion, 32 per cent or $18 billion was capitalized, and only $8 billion or 68 per cent of the production was consumed, while in 1944, 90 per cent of the production was consumed and only 10 per cent capitalized, it is indicated, I think, in order to see the trend of our national economy, to examine the same economic sectors at two different

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INCLUSION OF MENTAL HOSPITALS AND TUBERCULOSIS SANATORIA IN FEDERAL HOSPITAL INSURANCE PROGRAM
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of including mental hospitals and tuberculosis sanatoria in the federal hospital insurance program (Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act) so that the provinces will have available sufficient funds to provide for adequate treatment of the mentally ill, those people suffering from tuberculosis, and the care and training of mentally retarded children.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
He said: The motion which I move today is one which I have been moving for a number of years. The principle enunciated in this motion was endorsed by, and indeed the wording could have come from, the very fine report and recommendations of the Hall commission. In dealing with the problem of mental illness the commission said:
There must be an immediate end to the distinction that some still make in attitudes towards those who are mentally ill and those who are physically ill.
The commission points out that under the present terms of the hospital act, payment for the care of the mentally ill is excluded if provided in provincial mental hospitals but it is included if provided in general hospitals.
June 21, 19S7

They say further that they believe this policy of excluding the mentally ill is not in the public interest.
I want to deal with this point for a moment. The situation as it now exists has created a condition in which we have two types of treatment for the mentally ill. I am not suggesting for a moment that this was planned by any government nor that this was the intention of doctors or psychiatrists. However, if a person becomes ill and the doctor and the private psychiatrist, who are usually on the staff of a general hospital, whether it be the Winnipeg General Hospital or the Royal Victoria Hospital in Montreal or any of the hospitals in the larger cities in Canada, decide that the patient needs hospitalization, he can be admitted to the psychiatric ward of that general hospital. There he will get the finest of attention, the cost of which in any of our best hospitals is between $30 and $35 a day, and the entire cost for what we in Manitoba call standard care, is paid for by the government hospitalization program. I think this is as it should be.
Now, who are the people who usually see psychiatrists? They are people in the middle and upper income groups, people who are covered by non-profit medical insurance plans like the Manitoba Medical Service or P.S.I. in Ontario. If, on the other hand, a person who is in the lower income bracket, who, very often, does not have a doctor and who certainly does not frequent a private psychiatrist's office, gets sick, it is likely that he will be committed to the only place to which he can go, that is one of the provincial mental hospitals. In these hospitals the average cost of care per a day is not the $30 to $35 a day which we find in the general hospitals of the country but just under $8 a day. I suggest this is the kind of anomaly which should not be allowed to continue.
Having been in the provincial legislature of Manitoba, I have some concept of the difficulties which all the provinces have in meeting their tremendous responsibilities. The provincial governments, whether they be the "have" provinces such as Ontario and British Columbia or the "have not" provinces like Newfoundland or Nova Scotia, are having to find the money to pay for the cost of education, for a large part of the cost of welfare, and for part of the cost of hospitalization. The amounts of money which provincial governments have allocated for the treatment and care of the mentally ill in provincial institutions has risen very sharply.
DEBATES	1795
Mental and Tuberculosis Hospital Program However, 1 think it is obvious to all of us that there is a limit to what the provinces can do. What I am proposing in this resolution, and what the Hall commission has recommended very strongly, is that the mental hospitals be included in the provisions of the hospital insurance act so that the federal government would in effect pay for half the cost of the treatment of the mentally ill in hospital. What I am suggesting is not that the provinces should reduce their expenditures by half. I hope the federal government will adopt this principle, in fact I am certain they will if not now then in the not too distant future. I hope that in negotiations with the provinces the federal government will make it clear to the provinces that they are only prepared to extend the coverage for mental hospitals and for T.B. sanatoria if the provinces continue to spend the same amount of money as thej have been spending. So, in effect, what I am suggesting is that we double the expenditure which we make in this country for people who are mentally ill and who are required to spend time in mental hospitals.
I do not think there is any member of the house who will dispute the fact that there is a tremendous shortage of required facilities. I have brought with me today a couple of dozen, if not more, newspaper reports on this subject which I have accumulated. Here I have the Toronto Daily Star of January 19, 1967. A headline on the front page of that issue reads:	"Psychiatrist charges:	40 disturbed boys without proper treatment". I will read a couple of paragraphs from the article:
Forty emotionally disturbed youngsters have been kept in an Uxbridge training school in the past year without proper psychiatric treatment, a Toronto psychiatrist said last night.
Dr. John Rich, who Friday committed a 12-year-old boy from the St. John's Training School to the Ontario Hospital at Hamilton, said both institutions were "completely unsuitable".
Then, there is a story which appeared almost three years ago in the Winnipeg Tribune of September 11, 1964. The heading reads: "Nothing but jail for the sex offenders". I will read a short part of the article which reads as follows:
In Manitoba today, there are many men serving jail terms for crimes they couldn't help committing.
Wilbert X is an example: he's a sexual offender. He was convicted of gross indecency....
In sentencing him to the jail in Brandon, the magistrate said that he knew nothing would be done for this man in the jail in Brandon since they did not have the facilities.
June 21, 1967
1796	COMMONS
Mental and Tuberculosis Hospital Program There simply was no institution in the province of Manitoba which could handle the problems which this man had.
The statistics, of which there are many, give a graphic picture of the total situation in Canada. The Hall commission pointed out that 10 per cent of the population, about 1.9 million people, may be suffering from psychiatric and emotional disorders; that every day in Canada there are 69,000 people in mental institutions and that if you total the number in the year, there are 25 million days a year used in mental hospitals. The Hall commission estimates that mental illness accounts for almost 40 per cent of all hospital days, and in 1960 more than a third of all hospital beds in Canada were used for mentally ill patients. The figure has not changed much since that date.
As I have already pointed out, the cost of keeping and caring for a patient in a mental hospital is about a quarter of the cost of keeping a person in a general hospital. We get what we pay for. We get the kind of treatment, the kind of niggardly, miserable treatment, for which we pay. In the two provincial mental hospitals in Manitoba, the Brandon hospital and the Selkirk hospital, as of a year or two ago-I have not seen the most recent figures-there were more than 1,000 patients, and in each of these hospitals there were less than a dozen trained psychiatrists I remember when I was in the provincial legislature, and that was only five years ago, in one of the hospitals with 1,200 patients there were only three trained psychiatrists. If you keep in mind that one of them was the superintendent, who I am sure had a great deal of administrative work to do in the hospital, you can see, Mr. Speaker, that there was very little time for a psychiatrist to spend with individual patients. The result has been just what one might expect:	people stay in
hospitals for months, even years, when they could be at home if only they could receive individual attention.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
The Hall commission laid down certain principles with respect to mental hospitals which I think we ought to keep in mind. They pointed out that there are severe shortages of psychiatrists, psychologists, psychiatric nurses and social workers in all our mental institutions. The commission recommended a crash program for training personnel in this field. There is no place where these people can be trained better, more easily and more cheaply than in our mental hospitals, but this cannot


be done unless we are prepared to spend the amount of money required.
The Hall commission also called for increased funds for an expanded, co-ordinated program of research into the causes of mental illness and mental retardation. Mental illness is costing the people of Canada hundreds of millions of dollars a year in direct cost for the operation of our hospitals. There is also an indirect cost as a result of the thousands of people who are unable to work because of mental illness.
We are spending hundreds of millions of dollars on research, Mr. Speaker. We are doing research into how best to use our forests. We are doing research into how best to use our minerals. We are doing research into space exploration and into almost every field. The amount we spend on research in the field of mental illness is so small that one can hardly find the amount listed in the estimates for scientific research.
I am suggesting that if the federal government would participate in the hospital program in respect of the mentally ill, we could fairly easily commence the work on mental health research which is required.
Again, the Hall commission recommended that the hospital construction grant regulations under the health facilities development fund be amended to provide one half of the cost of construction of psychiatric wards in all general hospitals. It also recommended that henceforth all discrimination in the distinction between the mentally and physically ill in the organization and provision of services for their treatment, and the attitudes upon which these discriminations are based, be disavowed for all time as unworthy and unscientific.
In retrospect, Mr. Speaker, we can be critical of the federal government of the day, when it implemented the original hospitalization program and assumed 50 per cent of the cost of the program, for making the decision to exclude mental hospitals and T.B. sana-taria from the provisions of the act. However, I suppose I can understand this; the federal government knew that it was going to get into a program which would be very expensive.
Almost 20 years have past, and to a large extent the hospital building program has been met. I know that in some of the large cities such as Toronto, Montreal, Ottawa and Winnipeg there is still a shortage of hospital beds, but the bulk of the program has been implemented. I suggest that the time has long
June 21, 1967	COMMONS
since passed when the federal government should decide to include mental hospitals in the general program.
I want to close, Mr. Speaker, by putting on the record the views of Dr. Charles Roberts, who is now director of the Clarke Institute of Psychiatry in Toronto and who was for years head of the Verdun Protestant Hospital in Montreal. His views are reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail for January 11, 1966, and he had this to say:
A major frustration for psychiatric patients and workers is the conflict between statements that mental illness should be treated like any other disease and the refusal to make provisions to do so

Dr. Roberts said mental treatment should be included in hospital insurance programs. It has often been claimed since the program was introduced in 1957 that it was impossible to find the money at the federal level to include mental care, but since then there has been one of the greatest airport construction programs any country has ever undertaken; the trans-Canada highway has been financed and the St. Lawrence seaway has been completed. Hundreds of millions more dollars are being made available for universal old age pensions and the Canada Pension Plan.
I agree with Dr. Roberts. All of these things are needed. But so is an improvement in the facilities which are provided for the hundreds of thousands of people in Canada who are mentally ill and need assistance.
